public_rationale: The claim is modest: customers are starting to see the technology's limits. 2025 research backs it. BCG's September 2025 survey found 60% of companies getting 'hardly any material value' despite substantial investment. Gartner placed generative AI in the Trough of Disillusionment in 2025, a stage defined by disappointment after early hype. Wharton's 2025 survey cuts the other way: three in four leaders reported positive returns and most planned to spend more. But seeing limits is not the same as abandoning the technology, and BCG and Gartner both show growing awareness of shortfalls. On balance, the evidence supports the claim as worded.
limitations: The Gartner finding is cited through a news report because Gartner's pages were blocked.
Company surveys are self-reported, and the BCG and Wharton samples differ.

statement.document_title: “Scale Is All You Need” is dead

our_interpretation: Plain reading: in 2025, up to the post date, business users of generative AI were reporting disappointing value, weak returns or performance problems, which shows growing awareness of the technology's limits.
'Starting to' means a new or growing recognition. It does not require customers to abandon the technology.
criteria.support_condition: Customer surveys or analyst research from 2025 show many organisations reporting little value, weak ROI or disillusionment with generative AI.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Customer surveys from 2025 show most organisations satisfied, reporting strong value and no growing disappointment.

evidence.explanation: A large 2025 executive survey finds most companies reporting little value from AI despite heavy spending. That is customers running into the technology's limits in practice.

evidence.explanation: A survey of senior leaders at large US firms (fielded mid-2025) found most reporting positive returns and planning more spending. This tempers the claim, though recognising limits is compatible with positive returns.
